Today I'm interviewing Maria Dalton, who works as a TV sports presenter.
Hello.
What made you become a sports presenter?
I've always loved sports, doing things like training the women's football team at college.
People said I gave very clear instructions.
A guy who worked on a newspaper came to ask me questions for an article he was writing, and he suggested I'd make a good sports presenter.
I made up my mind I'd like to try it.
So I did a tour of the television studio to find out what it was like.
I see. Is the profession hard to get into?
Well, it's common to dream of working in sport on TV, so that means strong competition for jobs.
There are courses you can do, though they're quite expensive.
When you're presenting a sports programme on live TV, it's stressful in the studio with busy people all around you.
It's not just sitting in front of a camera.
How did you prepare for your first time on live TV?
I was nervous.
Everyone kept saying I should feel confident because I deserved the job, but I just couldn't believe it was happening.
I went for a long run, which made me feel calmer.
Afterwards, I felt really uncomfortable seeing the recording of myself, although I'm used to it now.
So what do you worry about when you're on TV?
There's always something for me.
It's suddenly not knowing what I'd plan to ask next.
When I'm talking to sports people, I have ideas written down, but sometimes a conversation changes and things go out of my head.
Some presenters make mistakes when they're trying to say long names and things, but that hasn't happened to me.
I hear you're doing a new TV programme soon.
Yes, I'm so excited.
I got the idea from watching kids in my hometown doing amazing new sports like underwater basketball.
So I'm going around the country having a go at some of these activities and we'll film teenagers doing their sports.
There may be some future champions.
Do you have advice for people interested in sports journalism?
Well, although everyone has favourite sports they can talk about for hours, you never know what you'll end up covering.
So knowledge about a variety is important.
And just don't think about TV.
Look for interview opportunities at local sports events,
or ask about positions in newspapers or radio, and watch what the experts in the profession do.
Thanks, Maria. Thank you.
